title: Wabash Blues: head arrangements, rehearsal and recording balance
summary: On Wabash Blues Albert says there were no written arrangements, numbers were rehearsed by ear for hours, and the mics favored reeds over trumpets and drove tuba prominence.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Were you using any written arrangements for this?
No written arrangements at all. Weren't too many arrangers in those days.
But the saxes sound together and everything. That's right.
Now, that's me blowing the soul away.
One trombone sustained, but Charlie Dixon doubling on his solos. Benny Long didn't do any solo work. It's Kelo Jefferson.
I know I got my dream. I know I got my dream.
I know I got my dream. I know I got my dream. I always tell Charlie Dixon's to be mixed practically the same changes in the sounds in his changes. Mm-hmm.
Yeah, the thing worked up for every tune.

That's right. Well, that's what the rehearsals were for. We'd possibly go sit down and rehearse maybe one or two numbers in two, three, four hours. Really? Playing these numbers, it wasn't a problem to get the harmony together because most of the guys did play actually by ear and instinct.
That tuba is sure a pronounced instrument on these records. Oh yeah.
Well they kept the mics close to the reed instruments. I don't know why they did it. They hadn't perfected any sense of balance. Yeah.
It's hard for me to hear the trumpets in there.
Right. The trumpets were kept in the background. They're supposed to be loud instruments. Now it doesn't make any difference.
